sections.h2: Where are Pasco County property records kept?
sections.html:
The Pasco County Clerk and Comptroller keeps them, in the Official Records. Deeds, mortgages, liens and recorded civil judgments all land in that one series, and the clerk's website is the place to search it.

The clerk's FAQ says civil judgments are recorded in the county's official records, which is why a judgment against a seller can show up in a title search. Two judicial centers take in-person business: the Robert D. Sumner Judicial Center at 38053 Live Oak Avenue, Suite 207 in Dade City, phone (352) 521-4542, and the West Pasco Judicial Center at 7530 Little Road, Suite 105 in New Port Richey, phone (727) 847-8031. Mail goes to P.O. Box 338, New Port Richey, FL 34656-0338. The FAQ gives office hours of 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, Monday through Friday, excluding holidays.

Ownership and assessment data sits elsewhere. The Pasco County Property Appraiser, which counts 335,946 real property parcels, runs the records search by parcel, and its Sale Instrument Type page decodes the deed codes you see in a sales history.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a document in Pasco County?
sections.html:
The clerk's FAQ prints $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page. Those amounts fit the state statute, which sets $5.00 and $4.00 as base charges and adds a $1.00 and $0.50 trust fund charge plus $4 a page for technology.

That recording charge is separate from the documentary stamp tax on a deed. Florida's statute puts that tax at 70 cents on each $100 of consideration for every county except Miami-Dade, and the Department of Revenue says all parties to the document are liable no matter who agrees to pay. The clerk collects it at the counter when the deed is recorded.

One surcharge detail matters for large documents: the statute charges an extra $1.00 per name beyond four, and a different rate for instruments larger than 14 by 8.5 inches. Ask the clerk to quote the charge before you submit anything unusual.

sections.h2: Which deeds and transfers need stamp tax in Pasco County?
sections.html:
Most deeds do, whether or not they are recorded. The Department of Revenue lists warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee's, life estate and deed in lieu of foreclosure deeds as taxable, along with agreements for deed and certificates of title.

There are exceptions. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is listed as not taxable, and a spousal homestead deed where the only consideration is a mortgage is exempt. The department also states that no specific exemption exists for transfers made for estate planning. A lady bird deed has its own treatment: a 2020 departmental advisement concluded that the deed in question transferred no present beneficial interest and so owed no stamp tax on those facts. Do not rely on that advisement without a closing attorney's read of your facts.

A deed must be in writing and signed in front of two subscribing witnesses, and Florida allows the witnessing by audio-video technology. A quitclaim between family members still counts as a change of ownership for assessment, which can reset a capped homestead value.

  • Taxable: warranty, special warranty, quit claim, life estate, deed in lieu.
  • Not taxable: personal representative's deed under a probated will.
  • Exempt: certain spousal and divorce deeds for the marital home.

sections.h2: How does the Pasco County clerk handle foreclosure sales and probate records?
sections.html:
The clerk runs foreclosure sales online and records the certificate of title that moves ownership. The FAQ says anyone may bid, but bidders must register on the Pasco Realauction site and keep a deposit with the clerk before the sale.

The deposit must be at least 5 percent of the estimated high bid for each property you hope to win. ACH deposits need four full business days to clear, wires one, and cash or cashier's checks must reach the clerk by 5 p.m. Eastern the business day before the sale. If no objection is filed, the clerk issues the certificate of title after 10 full days from the certificate of sale. It is recorded in the Official Records and transfers ownership.

On probate, the FAQ explains that probate converts assets to cash for beneficiaries and creditors and legally transfers real property. It adds that depositing a will with the clerk costs nothing. Probate proceeds in the circuit court of the county where the person lived or owned property.

sections.h2: How do I protect against property fraud in Pasco County?
sections.html:
Sign up for the clerk's Property Fraud Alert, which watches recorded liens, deeds and mortgages in your name. You can enroll on the alert website or by phone at 800-747-4600, according to the clerk's FAQ.

If an alert arrives, the FAQ says to run an Official Records search to see whether the document is yours. Notices of commencement and marriage licenses can trigger alerts too. If a recorded document is fraudulent, the clerk points you to the Pasco County Sheriff's Office non-emergency number, 727-847-8102.

The Property Appraiser separately takes reports of possible homestead fraud. A seller who has already left a house vacant for months can ask the clerk for the alert and keep a recent Official Records printout in the sale file.

sections.h2: What should I check in the records before selling a Pasco County house?
sections.html:
Pull the Official Records for the parcel and read every recorded item against your deed. Title companies do the same at closing, so finding a problem first gives you time to fix it.

  • The vesting deed: do the names and legal description match your records?
  • Mortgages and satisfactions: is each loan paid with a recorded release?
  • Liens and judgments: civil judgments are recorded in the Official Records.
  • Tax status: ask the Pasco Tax Collector, whose recent purchases page says it is updated from ownership-change notices sent by the Property Appraiser.

Delinquent tax gets a certificate in June and can be auctioned after two years, per the Tax Collector, so an old unpaid bill is worth settling before you list. A recorded tax deed application is the sign that a lien has aged out.

faqs.q: Who records deeds in Pasco County?
faqs.a: The Pasco County Clerk and Comptroller records deeds in the Official Records. Dade City and New Port Richey offices serve walk-in customers, and the office is open 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, Monday through Friday.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Pasco County?
faqs.a: The clerk's FAQ lists $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page. A deed also owes the state's documentary stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 of consideration.

faqs.q: Can I search Pasco County records for liens online?
faqs.a: Yes. The clerk's Official Records search covers recorded liens, deeds and mortgages, and civil judgments are recorded there too. The Property Appraiser's records search covers parcel and sales data.

faqs.q: How do I get a Pasco County fraud alert on my property?
faqs.a: Sign up through the clerk's Property Fraud Alert system, online or at 800-747-4600. The service flags liens, deeds and mortgages recorded under your name.

faqs.q: Does a quitclaim deed in Pasco County owe stamp tax?
faqs.a: Generally yes. The Department of Revenue lists quit claim deeds among taxable documents, and a transfer is a change of ownership that can reset a capped homestead assessment.
